turns.doctor_question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I guess what finally got me in here is... over these last few months, my mind just keeps jumping all over the place. Like, every time the CB radio chirps, or I see a new fuel price sign—which, by the way, did you see diesel is up another twelve cents over on Route 9? I swear, it's getting ridiculous out there. I was talking to this guy at the Flying J, Bob, he hauls lumber, and he was saying the exact same thing about the prices. Just highway robbery, honestly. 

But anyway, yeah, every little thing catches my attention, or I get this whole new idea in my head while I'm behind the wheel. And because of that, I'm missing details I normally never miss. Like, I'll completely overlook a client's delivery note, or I'll forget who I promised to call back. Just... can't seem to keep my focus on what I'm actually supposed to be doing, you know?

turns.doctor_question: Lately, have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it’s funny you ask about that. Most nights lately I’m sleeping maybe three or four hours, tops. Then I’m up way before daylight, just feeling completely ready to roll instead of worn out like you'd expect. 

Which is actually great for beating the morning rush out of the yard, honestly. I got on the interstate around 3:30 AM on Tuesday, and let me tell you, the sunrise coming up over the ridge was something else. Reminded me of this run I used to make down to Florida back in the late nineties, hauling patio furniture of all things. I had this old Peterbilt cab—no AC, just rolling the windows down, listening to the engine. Man, they really don't make trucks like that anymore. Everything now is all computerized and covered in sensors. You can't even fix a simple issue without plugging a laptop into the dash, it's a joke. My buddy Carl had his rig in the shop for three weeks just because of a faulty chip. Three weeks! 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, right, sleeping. But yeah, three or four hours, and I'm good to go. Don't feel tired at all.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, wandering from the topic of sleep to a long, unrelated story about hauling patio furniture in the 90s and modern truck computers, eventually forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly states he sleeps only three or four hours a night but feels 'completely ready to roll' and not tired at all.

turns.doctor_question: Lately, have you felt unusually confident or powerful, like you could do things other people can’t?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I wouldn't say I'm superhuman or anything, but... yeah, I guess I've been feeling pretty sharp. Like, just last week, I got it in my head that I could rebuild the whole driver training program for our yard myself. I mean, the way they run it now is just completely backward. I was telling my dispatcher, I could make it run better than the bosses ever could, even though, you know, corporate policy isn't exactly my lane. 

But speaking of corporate, you wouldn't believe the memos they've been sending out lately. It's like they think we're driving these rigs from a desk. They want us logging every single stop, even if it's just to kick the tires or grab a coffee. I mean, I remember back before electronic logs, you just kept a paper book and used your common sense. My old boss, Frank—God rest his soul—he used to say, "As long as the freight gets there and the wheels stay on, I don't care if you stop to pet a dog." Frank was a good guy. He actually bought me my first CB radio. It was a Cobra 29, classic model. I tuned that thing myself, had the antenna perfectly matched. You could talk skip all the way to Texas on a clear night. 

But anyway, yeah, the training program. I just feel like I see the whole picture right now, you know? Like I can fix things that nobody else even realizes are broken.

symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient expresses inflated self-confidence, believing they can rebuild the company's training program better than the bosses and fix things no one else realizes are broken.

turns.doctor_question: Have these changes been bad enough that they’ve caused serious problems at work or in your life?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely causing some friction, yeah. Like at work, I've had to have dispatch and the clients repeat details I really should have tracked the first time. And a couple of my sales follow-ups just totally slipped through the cracks because I was chasing way too many ideas at once. 

Which, you know, is frustrating because usually I'm the guy who remembers everything. Like this one client in Ohio, Henderson Manufacturing, I used to know their receiving guy's schedule by heart. Dave was his name. Big guy, always wore a Cleveland Browns hat, even when they were having a terrible season. Which, let's be honest, is most seasons. I remember one time I hauled a load of steel piping out there in a blizzard, white-knuckle driving the whole way on I-80. Took me an extra four hours, but Dave stayed late to unload me, even gave me a thermos of coffee for the ride back. That's the kind of relationship you build when you're on top of your game, you know? You take care of them, they take care of you. Now, half these new drivers don't even step out of the cab to say hello. It's all just scan a barcode and go. No personal touch anymore. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, the problems. Yeah, so work's been a bit messy. And at home... man, my wife and daughter, they've been walking on eggshells around me. I can just tell I'm adding strain to the house when I'm supposed to be the one helping out and keeping things steady.

symptom_reasoning.S060: The patient notes his wife and daughter are 'walking on eggshells' around him, strongly implying irritability and snappiness at home.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I'm not seeing ghosts or hearing voices or anything. My eyes and ears work just fine. Better than fine, actually. 

Like the other night, I was driving through the mountains in Pennsylvania, and I swear I could hear a loose belt on a rig three lanes over before I even saw him. You get an ear for that kind of thing after a while. It's like a sixth sense. Speaking of senses, you ever notice how different parts of the country actually smell different? Like, you cross the line into New Mexico and it's all dry dirt and sagebrush. But down in Louisiana, it's just heavy and wet, like old wood and swamp water. I had a run down to Baton Rouge back in '08, right before the recession really hit hard. Hauling a load of industrial fryers, if you can believe it. The guy receiving them was this character named Thibodeaux. Took me out for crawfish after we unloaded. Best meal I ever had on the road. You can't get crawfish like that up here, they just don't know how to season it right. It's all about the boil, you know? 

But yeah, no, I'm not seeing things that aren't there. Just regular stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the initial question about hallucinations into a long, unrelated story about driving, regional smells, and eating crawfish in Louisiana.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies seeing ghosts, hearing voices, or seeing things that aren't there.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been hospitalized because of these changes?
turns.patient_response:
Hospitalized? No, no, they haven't locked me up or anything. I mean, I've got a job to do, right? I can't be sitting in some hospital bed when there's freight that needs moving. 

Though, you know, hospitals... they always smell like bleach and old soup. I had to go to one back in, oh, must have been 2012, when I slipped on some ice at a truck stop outside Omaha. Busted my wrist pretty good. The nurse there, she was from this tiny town in Nebraska, told me all about how they used to have these huge county fairs. She said they'd deep-fry just about anything—candy bars, butter, you name it. I always thought that was a southern thing, but I guess folks in the Midwest like their grease, too. It's funny how you meet people like that when you're just trying to get a cast put on. She even drew a little smiley face on the fiberglass. My daughter thought that was the funniest thing when I got home. She was only, what, eight at the time? Time just flies. 

But no, to answer your question, no hospitals for this. I'm still out there driving, still keeping the wheels turning.

turns.doctor_question: Have you believed lately that you have special powers or a special mission that other people would say isn’t real?
turns.patient_response:
Special powers? No, I'm just a regular guy. I mean, I'm good at my job, but I'm not Superman or anything. Though, you know, sometimes I feel like I've got a sixth sense for traffic. Like I can just tell when a jam is coming up before the GPS even registers it. 

Speaking of traffic, you ever driven through Atlanta during rush hour? Man, it is a nightmare. I had a run down there last month, hauling a load of office furniture. Desks, chairs, filing cabinets—the heavy stuff. Anyway, I'm coming down I-75, and right around Kennesaw, traffic just stops dead. Turns out a truck carrying watermelons had tipped over. Watermelons everywhere! Just a sea of green and red all over the highway. People were actually getting out of their cars and trying to grab the ones that weren't smashed. I saw this one guy in a suit trying to carry three of them at once, dropped one right on his shiny leather shoe. I was stuck there for three hours, but it was almost worth it just for the entertainment value. You see the craziest things on the road, I swear. 

But yeah, no special missions or powers. Just me and the truck, trying to get from point A to point B.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks at length, going off on a long, unprompted story about a traffic jam and spilled watermelons.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having any special powers or a special mission, stating he is just a regular guy.
